label: Fermented Iron-Jaggery Black Paste
formWords: Thick smooth paste in a shallow tray. The earlier ferment is a different look: rusted drums with a crusted grey-black skin, not what is printed.
colourWords: Very dark brown-black with a violet cast in the tray, wet and glossy, seen in one photo shoot. #2B211B is a slightly warm approximation of it. On harde cloth a just-printed area looks glossy and dark (a reading of the sheen); a dried museum stage sample reads only taupe-brown, and the GI and Karolia place full black later, on cloth.
renderNote: Photo: About Amazon India, one shoot by Jan Sassmannshausen. dye.jpg (carousel label 'Step 4: Resist Print', paste not named) reads flat fill #231716, darker #19110F and wall #2A1C20; bt6a2087.jpg, captioned 'A worker using the black dye to print on a fabric', shows the same kind of tray with a violet-black rim (#221E23). Near-neutral cloth in both frames argues the violet cast is real in that shoot. #2B211B is slightly lighter and warmer than those medians; #2A1C20 carries the cast. Camera value under that photo's own light, not albedo.
basis: Photo, one Amazon shoot: one tray photo with a conflicting carousel label plus one captioned black-dye photo showing the tray edge. The GI and D'source support the process and the tray, not the shade.
variation: Thickener differs by source: tamarind seed in most, tree gum at GI PDF p. 6 (one text family with Wandering Silk); no visible difference. Dried print from taupe #9C8366 (Crafts Museum stage sample, scan) to #191B23 (Assal, cool phone shot). Project LooM records alum added for a grey tone. Sources disagree on when it reaches full black.
surfaceWords: Smooth, thick, wet and glossy, with no visible scrap: the iron stays behind in the ferment. Tray walls and rim carry dark crust; a mesh-like dimpled pattern shows in one frame.

conflicts.question: The GI (PDF p. 6) describes a fermented paste of jaggery, iron and besan; dranshublog describes drained liquid boiled with tamarind seed powder.
conflicts.outcome: Settled at high confidence as one process in two stages: the GI's next sentence says the resulting iron water is drained off and mixed with smooth tree gum paste, and practitioner and academic accounts give the same sequence.
conflicts.unsettled: The thickener: tamarind seed has several independent witnesses, while tree gum appears only at GI PDF p. 6 and Wandering Silk, one text family; it makes no visible difference. The wet paste's colour in the tray is described by no source. How fast and how far the printed line darkens differs between sources: the GI says it develops, and black develops at rang; Karolia and Buch place permanent black at indigo.

conflicts.question: FAO's monograph is potassium alum, while dranshublog calls Ajrakh's alum aluminium sulphate.
conflicts.outcome: Not settled, low to medium confidence. No source read identifies the alum in a present-day workshop by analysis; registry and field sources say only fatakdi (alum). Nineteenth-century Kutch-made alum was a potash double salt (Bombay Gazetteer V and Watt, one witness), and its use by Ajrakh printers is inferred. For today's workshops there is no lean either way. The aluminium sulphate reading traces to a bracketed reading in one 2012 blog by a workshop-taught researcher, repeated by others, and one general statement by Jenny Dean. The Bagru and Sanganeri GI documents name aluminium sulphate for the printed mordant (one witness between them).
conflicts.unsettled: The chemical type. Watt's 1878 assay (10.73 per cent alumina with 13 per cent impurities) argues against plain sulphate but reports no potassium determination. The appearance is taken by analogy from other crafts and a chemical monograph, so translucent or milky crystalline lumps would be as defensible as clear crystals.

Burial is attested at one Pedana workshop family and in S4, whose independence from that workshop is unproven; depth differs between their accounts; above ground rests on one 1982 photo with no stated place; the Census, the GI and Sengupta are silent. conflicts.question: S4 (PDF p. 5) calls karakkaya dried flowers; S6, the Ajrakh GI and other sources use the dried fruit of Terminalia chebula.
conflicts.outcome: The word means the fruit: C. P. Brown's Telugu-English Dictionary (1903) gives karaka as the yellow myrobalan, Terminalia chebula, and karakkaya as its fruit, and the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia lists Karakkaya as a Telugu synonym in the fruit monograph. The mordant bath is dried fruit at medium to high confidence: a named Polavaram dyer (Sengupta, form-feed p. 94) and a first-person Pedana account both contradict flowers for the bath, so S4's flowers is taken as an error for the bath.
conflicts.unsettled: The material for the yellow is disputed: the same Polavaram dyer says one myrobalan material does tanning and yellow ('seeds', his word), against S4 p. 11 and a partly copied chain of flower statements. What a 'myrobalan flower' physically is (true flower or leaf gall) stays open. The liquid's colour is not settled.
